runs.report:
## CRISPR Base Editing vs. Prime Editing: A Comparative Report

CRISPR-Cas systems have revolutionized genome editing, offering precise tools for various applications, from disease modeling to gene therapy. Among the advanced iterations, base editing (BE) and prime editing (PE) stand out for their ability to modify DNA without inducing double-strand breaks (DSBs), a key advantage over earlier CRISPR methods. This report summarizes the distinctions and applications of these two sophisticated editing technologies.

### Mechanisms and Capabilities

**Base Editing (BE)**

*   **Mechanism:** Utilizes catalytically impaired Cas proteins (e.g., dCas9 variants) fused to a deaminase enzyme [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624). This system chemically modifies a single base, directly converting it to another, without requiring a DSB or a donor DNA template [source](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
*   **Editing Types:**
    *   **Cytosine Base Editors (CBEs):** Facilitate C to T conversions [source](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
    *   **Adenine Base Editors (ABEs):** Facilitate A to G conversions [source](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
    *   **Glycosylase Base Editors (GBEs):** Facilitate C to G conversions [source](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
    *   **Dual-Base Editors (DBEs):** Can perform simultaneous C to T and A to G conversions [source](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
*   **Specificity:** Primarily limited to specific base substitutions [source](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z).

**Prime Editing (PE)**

*   **Mechanism:** Employs a fused Cas9 nickase and a reverse transcriptase, guided by a prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA). The pegRNA specifies the target site and carries the desired edit, which is then reverse transcribed into the target DNA without DSBs or external donor DNA [source](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z), [source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).
*   **Editing Types:** Offers a broader range of modifications compared to BE, enabling:
    *   All types of DNA point mutations [source](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
    *   Small insertions [source](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
    *   Small deletions [source](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
    *   Large deletions (up to ~1 kb, with some reported up to ~10 kb) and insertions (up to ~40 bp) with specialized variants [source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).
    *   Complex genome rearrangements [source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).
*   **Specificity:** Allows for programmable "search-and-replace" functionality, offering a broad framework for targeted sequence rewriting [source](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z).

### Applications

**Both BE and PE**

*   **Broad Applicability:** Used across bacteria, plants, animals, and microorganisms [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624), [source](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
*   **Research & Development:** Accelerate research in synthetic biology, agriculture, metabolism, and biomedicine [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).
*   **Gene Therapy & Disease Modeling:** Utilized for gene therapy, disease modeling, agronomic trait development, and stress resistance [source](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
*   **Clinical Potential:** Moving from research to clinic, with CRISPR-derived treatments approved for β-hemoglobinopathies and expanding across various diseases [source](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports-medicine/fulltext/S2666-3791%2825%2900532-4). Examples include personalized base editing for rare metabolic disorders [source](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports-medicine/fulltext/S2666-3791%2825%2900532-4).

### Limitations and Challenges

**Both BE and PE**

*   **PAM Specificity:** Target site constraints due to protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) specificity, although newer variants of Cas proteins are expanding targeting options [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).
*   **Editing Efficiency:** Efficiency can vary and is generally lower for some variants, though newer editors show improved performance [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624). Early PE variants (PE1) showed low efficiency (0.7%–5.5%) [source](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
*   **Off-Target Effects:** While generally exhibiting fewer indels than DSB-based editing, off-target edits can still occur. Mitigation strategies include high-fidelity Cas9 fusions and optimized guide RNA design [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).
*   **Delivery:** Achieving efficient, tissue-specific, and transient in vivo delivery remains a central challenge, along with minimizing immune responses [source](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports-medicine/fulltext/S2666-3791%2825%2900532-4).
*   **Safety and Efficacy:** Require ongoing evaluation for cytotoxicity, immune responses, long-term safety, and tissue/context-dependent risks [source](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports-medicine/fulltext/S2666-3791%2825%2900532-4).

**Specific to BE**

*   **Off-Target Mutations:** BE has shown more off-target mutations compared to PE in some studies, though engineered variants have reduced Cas9-independent off-targeting [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).

**Specific to PE**

*   **Off-Target Activity:** While early PE variants (PE2/PE3) showed lower off-target editing than Cas9, nuclease-based PEn/uPEn can exhibit off-targets similar to Cas9 nuclease, emphasizing the need for high-fidelity enzymes and careful pegRNA design [source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).
*   **Genome Instability:** Potential for genome instability from perturbations to DNA repair processes requires careful assessment [source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).

### Conclusion

Both base editing and prime editing represent significant advancements in precise genome modification, offering DSB-free approaches with broad applicability. While base editing is limited to specific base-to-base conversions, prime editing offers a more versatile "search-and-replace" capability, allowing for all types of point mutations, and small to large insertions and deletions. Both technologies face ongoing challenges in efficiency, off-target effects, and delivery, but continuous innovation promises to enhance their precision, versatility, and therapeutic potential.

## CRISPR Base Editing vs. Prime Editing: A Comparative Report

CRISPR/Cas systems have revolutionized genome editing, leading to the development of precise tools like base editing (BE) and prime editing (PE). Both aim to achieve specific DNA modifications without creating double-strand breaks (DSBs), thereby reducing the risk of undesirable insertions and deletions (indels). This report outlines the differences, applications, and limitations of these two advanced editing technologies.

### Mechanisms and Capabilities

**Base Editing (BE)**

*   **Mechanism:** Base editors utilize a catalytically impaired Cas protein (e.g., dCas9 variant) fused to a deaminase enzyme. They directly convert one DNA base into another (e.g., C to T, or A to G) without cutting both DNA strands [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).
*   **Capabilities:**
    *   Enables precise, DSB-free genome modifications at single-base resolution [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).
    *   Has seen significant improvements in efficiency, targeting scope, and specificity since its emergence around 2016 [source](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-026-01548-7).
    *   Newer editors like ABE8e and BE4 show improved performance [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).

**Prime Editing (PE)**

*   **Mechanism:** Prime editing employs a programmable pegRNA-guided system that uses a reverse transcriptase to directly "write" new genetic information into a target DNA site. It typically creates a single-strand nick (not a DSB) and recruits reverse transcription to install edits, eliminating the need for a donor DNA template [source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).
*   **Capabilities:**
    *   Offers higher precision than standard CRISPR-Cas9 [source](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03371-x).
    *   Can perform a wider range of edits compared to base editing, including insertions, deletions, and all 12 possible point mutations, as well as more complex genome rearrangements [source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/, https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03371-x).
    *   New editor variants (TwinPE, GRAND, PRIME-Del, HOPE, Bi-PE) enable deletions up to ~1 kb and insertions up to ~40 bp, with some methods reporting larger deletions (e.g., ~10 kb) [source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).
    *   Achieves 30-80% efficiency for certain deletions in cell lines and precise deletions up to ~780 nt [source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).

### Applications

**Base Editing (BE)**

*   Used in clinical trials for conditions such as sickle cell disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, inborn errors of metabolism, certain leukemias, and cardiovascular indications [source](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-026-01548-7).
*   Supports therapeutic development through both ex vivo (edited patient cells) and in vivo approaches [source](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-026-01548-7, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10532350/).
*   Has applications in bacteria, plants, and other systems, accelerating research in synthetic biology, agriculture, and metabolism [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).

**Prime Editing (PE)**

*   Demonstrated in vivo gene editing in a human body for the first time to treat Wilson disease, targeting liver cells to correct the ATP7B gene [source](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03371-x).
*   Has therapeutic potential, with workflows like PEDAR demonstrating precise correction of a pathogenic insertion in a mouse model of tyrosinemia [source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).
*   Also has broad applications across bacteria, plants, and other systems, accelerating research in synthetic biology, agriculture, and metabolism [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).

### Limitations and Challenges

**Base Editing (BE)**

*   **Target site constraints:** Limited by PAM specificity, though alternative Cas proteins are expanding targeting [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).
*   **Off-target effects:** Can exhibit off-target mutations, though typically fewer indels than DSB-based methods. Cas9-independent off-targeting has been reduced by engineered variants [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).
*   **Efficiency:** Editing efficiency can vary and is generally lower for some variants [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).

**Prime Editing (PE)**

*   **Delivery challenges:** Ongoing discussions emphasize the difficulties in delivering PE components to target cells [source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).
*   **Potential genome instability:** Perturbations to DNA repair processes could lead to genome instability [source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).
*   **Off-target considerations:** While early PE variants (PE2/PE3) showed lower off-target editing than Cas9, nuclease-based PEn/uPEn can exhibit off-targets similar to Cas9 nuclease, necessitating high-fidelity enzymes and careful pegRNA design [source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/). PE generally demonstrates notably lower off-target changes (~0.6% on average) at tested loci compared to DSB methods and fewer off-target mutations than BE [source](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).
*   **Safety evaluation:** Important to evaluate insertions/deletions, scaffold-derived mutations, and overall genomic integrity [source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).

### Outlook

Both base editing and prime editing are rapidly advancing tools with strong potential for therapeutic applications and diverse research areas. Continued optimization is crucial to broaden their target scope, boost efficiency, and minimize off-target effects. AI is also playing an increasing role in optimizing these tools by assisting with editor selection, gRNA design, off-target assessment, and even de novo editor design [source](https://www.cell.com/molecular-cell/fulltext/S1097-2765(26)00594-0). As these technologies mature, responsible development, regulatory oversight, and ethical considerations remain paramount to ensure safe and equitable translation to clinical use [source](https://www.cell.com/molecular-cell/fulltext/S1097-2765(26)00594-0, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10532350/).

Summary:
- Mercury is a naturally occurring but highly toxic element that threatens health, especially fetal and early-life development.
- Human exposure occurs mainly via inhalation of mercury vapors (industrial settings) and consumption of methylmercury in fish and shellfish; inorganic and organic forms have varying toxic effects affecting the nervous, digestive, immune systems, lungs, kidneys, skin, and eyes.

Essential results from EPA on health effects of mercury exposure:

- Mercury types and exposure risk:
  - Methylmercury (primarily from eating contaminated fish/shellfish) is a powerful neurotoxin. Most people have trace amounts; high exposure can cause adverse health effects. Unborn infants are particularly vulnerable, as prenatal exposure can affect brain and nervous system development, with lasting impacts on cognitive function, memory, attention, language, fine motor skills, and visual-spatial skills.
  - Metallic (elemental) mercury exposure occurs mainly via inhalation of mercury vapor (e.g., spills or broken devices). Acute/long-term inhalation can cause tremors, mood changes, insomnia, neuromuscular issues, headaches, sensory disturbances, and impaired cognitive function; higher exposures can affect kidneys, respiration, and can be fatal.
  - Inorganic mercury exposure (from some industrial sources or ingestion) can damage the gastrointestinal tract, nervous system, and kidneys. Symptoms may include skin rashes, mood swings, memory loss, mental disturbances, and muscle weakness. All mercury forms can be absorbed via the GI tract, with systemic effects.

- Factors influencing health outcomes:
  - Mercury form (methylmercury, elemental, inorganic)
  - Dose/exposure level
  - Age (unborn infants most vulnerable)
  - Duration of exposure
  - Route of exposure (inhalation, ingestion, skin contact)
  - Individual health status

- General guidance:
  - Most people’s blood mercury levels are below levels associated with health effects, but high methylmercury exposure can still cause harm.
  - If concerned about exposure, consult a physician or poison control (1-800-222-1222).

- Related point on drinking water:
  - EPA sets maximum contaminant levels (MCLs) to limit mercury in drinking water, balancing health protection with feasibility; some states may enforce stricter limits.

Summary:

Mercury has multiple exposure forms with overlapping neurological and renal toxicity observed in humans and animals.

Key form-specific health effects:

- Elemental mercury (vapor exposure)
  - Neurological: tremor, impaired motor function and coordination, memory and cognitive performance decrements, mood and neuropsychiatric symptoms.
  - Renal: evidence of glomerular and tubular injury.
  - Other notes: severe respiratory effects (pneumonitis, pulmonary edema) reported in fatal/near-fatal inhalation cases.
  - Epidemiology: adults show neurological effects; some animal data on neurodevelopment and CNS effects.

- Inorganic mercury salts
  - Neurological: strong neurodevelopmental effects (hyperactivity, impaired coordination, memory, sociability) and adult neurobehavioral signs (ataxia, tremor, paralysis) with CNS neuropathology.
  - Renal: dose- and duration-dependent nephrotoxicity (proximal/distal tubules, glomerular damage, brush border loss).
  - Cardiovascular: elevated blood pressure, altered cardiac function.
  - Immunological: immune stimulation in susceptible strains.
  - Reproductive: impaired fertility, reduced sperm quality.
  - Cancer: some evidence of carcinogenicity in male rats (forestomach/thyroid).
  - Epidemiology: no direct epidemiologic studies for inorganic mercury salts; animal data robust for multiple organ systems.

- General cardiovascular findings (across mercury exposure)
  - Biomarker-associated studies show associations with higher blood pressure and various cardiovascular outcomes in humans, across occupational elemental exposure and methylmercury from fish.

Overall pattern:
- Neurological and renal toxicity are consistently observed across mercury forms in both humans and animals.
- Inorganic mercury shows broader systemic effects (cardiovascular, immunological, reproductive, potential cancer signals in animals).
- Elemental mercury vapor primarily concerns neurological and renal effects, plus severe respiratory injury at very high exposure.
- Cardiovascular data are heterogeneous but indicate potential blood pressure and functional changes with mercury exposure.

If you want, I can tailor the summary to focus on a specific form (elemental, inorganic) or to extract the risk types (neuro, renal, cardiovascular) with bulleting by exposure scenario.

# Mercury Safety Report

## Health Risks of Mercury Exposure

Mercury is a naturally occurring element that is highly toxic and poses significant health threats, particularly to fetal and early-life development [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/). Human exposure primarily occurs through inhaling mercury vapors in industrial settings and consuming methylmercury found in fish and shellfish [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/). Different forms of mercury have varying toxic effects on multiple body systems, including the nervous, digestive, immune systems, lungs, kidneys, skin, and eyes [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).

### Types of Mercury and Their Health Impacts

*   **Methylmercury**
    *   Primarily acquired from eating contaminated fish and shellfish [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   It is a powerful neurotoxin [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Unborn infants are particularly vulnerable, as prenatal exposure can impact brain and nervous system development, leading to lasting effects on cognitive function, memory, attention, language, fine motor skills, and visual-spatial skills [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   High exposure can cause neurological and behavioral damage [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
*   **Metallic (Elemental) Mercury**
    *   Exposure mainly occurs through inhaling mercury vapor, such as from spills or broken devices [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Acute or long-term inhalation can cause tremors, mood changes, insomnia, neuromuscular issues, headaches, sensory disturbances, and impaired cognitive function [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Higher exposures can affect kidneys and respiration and may be fatal [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Severe respiratory effects, such as pneumonitis and pulmonary edema, have been reported in fatal or near-fatal inhalation cases [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
*   **Inorganic Mercury**
    *   Exposure can result from some industrial sources or ingestion [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Can damage the gastrointestinal tract, nervous system, and kidneys [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Symptoms may include skin rashes, mood swings, memory loss, mental disturbances, and muscle weakness [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
    *   Exhibits strong neurodevelopmental effects (e.g., hyperactivity, impaired coordination, memory, sociability) and adult neurobehavioral signs (e.g., ataxia, tremor, paralysis) [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
    *   Causes dose- and duration-dependent nephrotoxicity, including damage to proximal/distal tubules and glomeruli [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
    *   Can lead to elevated blood pressure and altered cardiac function [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
    *   Associated with impaired fertility and reduced sperm quality [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
    *   Some evidence suggests carcinogenicity in male rats (forestomach/thyroid) [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).

### General Health Outcomes and Considerations

*   Neurological and renal toxicity are consistently observed across all mercury forms in both humans and animals [source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
*   Factors influencing health outcomes include the mercury form, dose/exposure level, age (unborn infants are most vulnerable), duration and route of exposure, and individual health status [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
*   Most people's blood mercury levels are below levels associated with health effects, but high methylmercury exposure can still cause harm [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
*   Ethylmercury, found in thiomersal in some vaccines, is not considered a health risk [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
*   Mercury cannot be destroyed, emphasizing the importance of reducing its mining and use, particularly in artisanal gold mining, and promoting safer alternatives [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
*   Major sources of mercury emissions include burning coal and the improper disposal of mercury-containing devices and products such as batteries, thermometers, lamps, dental amalgam, cosmetics, and pharmaceuticals [source](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).

## Mercury Safety Regulations and Guidelines

Efforts are being made globally to manage and reduce mercury exposure through various regulations and initiatives.

*   The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) sets maximum contaminant levels (MCLs) to limit mercury in drinking water, aiming to balance health protection with feasibility, with some states enforcing stricter limits [source](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury).
*   The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) provides resources and documents related to the long-term management and storage of elemental mercury [source](https://www.energy.gov/em/long-term-management-and-storage-elemental-mercury).
*   Canada's National Strategy for Safe and Environmentally Sound Disposal of Lamps Containing Mercury Act (S.C. 2017, c. 16) establishes a framework for the safe collection, handling, treatment, and disposal of mercury-containing lamps [source](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/N-16.8/index.html). This Act aims to prevent mercury releases and reduce environmental and human health risks by promoting environmentally sound disposal practices, including extended producer responsibilities [source](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/N-16.8/index.html).
*   India is accelerating its efforts to eliminate mercury-containing medical devices, such as thermometers and blood pressure monitors, from public healthcare by 2030 [source](https://www.who.int/india/news-room/detail/22-10-2026-push-to-eliminate-mercury-based-devices-in-health-care). Key steps include replacing devices, strengthening mercury waste management, ensuring safe disposal, and providing access to alternatives [source](https://www.who.int/india/news-room/detail/22-10-2026-push-to-eliminate-mercury-based-devices-in-health-care). A national multi-sector strategy is in place, with many states completing inventories and issuing phase-out orders [source](https://www.who.int/india/news-room/detail/22-10-2026-push-to-eliminate-mercury-based-devices-in-health-care).

Summary:

Mercury has multiple exposure forms with overlapping neurological and renal toxicity observed in humans and animals.

Key form-specific health effects:

- Elemental mercury (vapor exposure)
  - Neurological: tremor, impaired motor function and coordination, memory and cognitive performance decrements, mood and neuropsychiatric symptoms.
  - Renal: evidence of glomerular and tubular injury.
  - Other notes: severe respiratory effects (pneumonitis, pulmonary edema) reported in fatal/near-fatal inhalation cases.
  - Epidemiology: adults show neurological effects; some animal data on neurodevelopment and CNS effects.

- Inorganic mercury salts
  - Neurological: strong neurodevelopmental effects (hyperactivity, impaired coordination, memory, sociability) and adult neurobehavioral signs (ataxia, tremor, paralysis) with CNS neuropathology.
  - Renal: dose- and duration-dependent nephrotoxicity (proximal/distal tubules, glomerular damage, brush border loss).
  - Cardiovascular: elevated blood pressure, altered cardiac function.
  - Immunological: immune stimulation in susceptible strains.
  - Reproductive: impaired fertility, reduced sperm quality.
  - Cancer: some evidence of carcinogenicity in male rats (forestomach/thyroid).
  - Epidemiology: no direct epidemiologic studies for inorganic mercury salts; animal data robust for multiple organ systems.

- General cardiovascular findings (across mercury exposure)
  - Biomarker-associated studies show associations with higher blood pressure and various cardiovascular outcomes in humans, across occupational elemental exposure and methylmercury from fish.

Overall pattern:
- Neurological and renal toxicity are consistently observed across mercury forms in both humans and animals.
- Inorganic mercury shows broader systemic effects (cardiovascular, immunological, reproductive, potential cancer signals in animals).
- Elemental mercury vapor primarily concerns neurological and renal effects, plus severe respiratory injury at very high exposure.
- Cardiovascular data are heterogeneous but indicate potential blood pressure and functional changes with mercury exposure.

Summary:

- Mercury is a naturally occurring element found in air, water, and soil; human exposure occurs mainly via inhalation of mercury vapour (industrial) and consumption of contaminated fish and shellfish (methylmercury).
- All humans have some level of exposure. Mercury poses health risks, especially to fetal and early child development, and can affect the nervous, digestive, immune systems, lungs, kidneys, skin, and eyes.
- Mercury exists in several forms (elemental, inorganic, organic like methyl- and ethylmercury) with differing toxic effects. Methylmercury from fish is a key exposure concern; ethylmercury (in thiomersal) used in some vaccines does not pose health risks.
- Health impacts include neurological and behavioral disorders, tremors, memory loss, cognitive/motor dysfunction, kidney damage, and skin problems. Inorganic mercury salts are corrosive to skin/eyes and can cause kidney toxicity.
- Public health actions emphasized: eliminate mercury mining and reduce use in mining (especially artisanal small-scale gold mining); promote non-mercury gold extraction; recycle existing mercury; replace mercury-containing devices and products; reduce emissions from coal-fired power plants and other sources; ensure safe disposal and use of safer alternatives; vaccines with thiomersal are not a health risk.
- Common sources and products containing mercury include batteries, thermometers/other measuring devices, electrical switches, lamps, dental amalgams, cosmetics, and certain pharmaceuticals.

If you need a shorter one-liner: Mercury exposure is common and health-threatening, especially to fetal development; main risks come from methylmercury in fish and elemental mercury from industrial sources, with strong emphasis on reducing mercury use and exposure and clarifying vaccine thiomersal safety.

Summary:
- Mercury exposes three chemical forms with overlapping health concerns, mainly neurological and renal effects across humans and animals.
- Elemental mercury (vapor):
  - Neurological effects in adults: tremor, vision and cognitive declines, slowed motor function, mood and behavioral changes.
  - Renal effects: decrements in kidney function; tubular and glomerular damage observed in animals and some human data.
  - Severe elemental mercury exposure can cause acute respiratory injury (pneumonitis, edema) and sometimes fatal outcomes.
- Inorganic mercury salts:
  - Neurological effects: developmental neurotoxicity (hyperactivity, impaired motor and memory, reduced sociability); adult neurobehavioral and motor impairments; overt signs in animals (ataxia, tremor, paralysis) and CNS changes.
  - Renal effects: dose- and duration-dependent nephrotoxicity (tubular and glomerular damage).
  - Cardiovascular effects: possible blood pressure and cardiac function changes.
  - Immunological and reproductive effects: immune activation in susceptible strains; impaired fertility and reduced sperm quality in animals.
  - Cancer: some evidence of male rat carcinogenicity (forestomach, thyroid); no clear human epidemiology.
- Cardiovascular findings (across mercury forms): some associations with increased blood pressure and altered cardiovascular function; evidence varies by exposure type (elemental, methylmercury, unspecified).
- Overall pattern: neurological and renal toxicity are the most consistently observed outcomes in both humans and animals; other organ systems show organ-specific or species-specific effects with more limited epidemiological support.

Mercury health effects depend on form (methylmercury, elemental/metallic, inorganic), dose, exposure duration, age (fetuses and young children are most vulnerable), and route of exposure. Key points:

- Methylmercury: most commonly from eating contaminated fish/shellfish. Most people have low body levels; high exposure can cause neurotoxic effects. Prenatal exposure can harm fetal brain/nervous system and later cognitive/behavioral functions. Possible symptoms: loss of peripheral vision, tingling, poor coordination, speech/hearing/walking impairment, and muscle weakness. If concerned, consult a physician.

- Metallic (elemental) mercury: risks mainly from inhaling mercury vapor. Symptoms with acute/long exposure include tremors, mood changes, insomnia, neuromuscular issues, headaches, sensory disturbances, cognitive decline; higher exposures can cause kidney damage, respiratory failure, or death.

- Inorganic mercury: high exposure can damage gastrointestinal tract, nervous system, kidneys; skin rashes, mood/memory changes, mental disturbances, muscle weakness. Absorption occurs via the GI tract.

- General guidance: exposure effects vary by form, dose, duration, age, and exposure route. Most people should consult a physician or poison control if exposure concerns arise (Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222). EPA drinking-water MCLs regulate inorganic mercury to prevent short- and long-term health risks.

Summary:
- Topic: Mercury in communities, focusing on old mercury-containing medical devices (thermometers, manual BP machines) and other mercury-containing products (cosmetics, electronics, medical waste, dental fillings, fluorescent lights, batteries, skin-lightening products).
- What mercury is: A naturally occurring, highly poisonous metal found in certain healthcare equipment and consumer products.
- Health risks: Mercury can damage kidneys, brain, lungs, immune system, and developing fetuses; pregnant women and children are especially vulnerable.
- Routes of exposure: Inhalation of contaminated air, ingestion of contaminated food, and skin contact.
- Common exposure sources in the community: Medical equipment (thermometers, BP machines), dental fillings, fluorescent tubes, batteries, skin-lightening products, medical waste, gold processing with mercury, waste sites, electrical switches, leather tanning.
- Symptoms of exposure: Headache, dizziness, cough, eye irritation, nausea, tremors, memory problems, mood changes, kidney and nervous system disorders, developmental issues in children, miscarriage.
- At-risk groups: Health workers (dentists, lab staff), healthcare cleaners, waste handlers, people near open dumpsites, users of skin-lightening products, people near gold mining, gold miners using mercury, leather tanners, traders dealing with mercury-containing equipment.
- Environmental spread: Mercury contaminates air, soil, and water; bioaccumulates in wildlife and can cause long-term harm to people.
- Immediate action if exposed: Seek prompt assessment and treatment at a health facility.
- Prevention tips: Avoid handling unidentified mercury-containing waste without PPE; wear nitrile gloves; wash hands after handling waste; do not dispose of mercury-containing items in rivers, drains, ordinary trash; do not burn or bury mercury-containing items; seek supervisor guidance if items break.

Resumen esencial:

- El mercurio es altamente tóxico y afecta gravemente el desarrollo cerebral de fetos y niños; daña sistemas nervioso, inmunitario, digestivo, así como pulmones y riñones.
- Vías principales de exposición: inhalación de vapores, ingestión de alimentos contaminados (especialmente peces grandes y depredadores), y contacto en piel con cosméticos o productos dudosos que contengan mercurio inorgánico; el embarazo y la lactancia permiten transmisión al feto y al bebé.
- Efectos en la salud: daño neurológico (temblores, problemas de coordinación, visión, memoria, aprendizaje, cambios de ánimo), daño renal, irritación de vías respiratorias y mucosas, y mayor riesgo de aborto espontáneo con alta exposición.
- Medidas preventivas en el hogar: usar tecnologías digitales (termómetros, tensiómetros) y retirar instrumentos de vidrio con mercurio; evitar almacenar, manipular o quemar mercurio líquido en viviendas.
- Protocolo ante rotura de un termómetro: ventilar; no usar escobas ni aspiradoras; recoger con guantes y papel rígido; colocar las esferas en frasco hermético.
- Alimentación segura: limitar consumo de pescados grandes y depredadores (tiburón, pez espada, caballa gigante; en ríos: zúngaro, doncella, mota punteada); preferir pescados pequeños para reducir acumulación de mercurio.

Fuente: Ministerio de Salud del Perú (Guía de prevención de riesgos por exposición a mercurio).

Summary:
- The page explains how heavy metals (notably mercury and lead) reach people through four main routes: air, soil/play surfaces, water (private wells), and local fish.
- Key practical steps:
  - Air/inhalation: reduce sources, use particle filtration (HEPA) and follow local guidance; HEPA helps with dust and outdoor pollution events, but not mercury vapor (gas). For mercury spills, isolate the area and follow EPA/ Poison Control instructions.
  - Soil and dust: avoid contact with bare soil, use clean play surfaces, wash hands, remove shoes at the door; wet-wipe and HEPA-vacuum for lead dust; avoid dry sweeping.
  - Water wells: test for relevant contaminants; choose treatment based on results; natural arsenic/uranium can be concerns even away from industry.
  - Fish and seafood: check local fish advisories before consuming; use seafood guides to choose lower-mercury options.
- Mercury pathway: coal burning releases mercury → deposition on land/water → methylmercury formed by microorganisms → bioaccumulates in aquatic food webs; closest plant alone doesn’t indicate fish mercury levels; consult advisories.
- Additional resources: review local air conditions, check EPA/agency data on releases and permits, examine soil/water cleanup records, and keep testing/advisory instructions for wells and seafood.
- Practical actions:
  - Open the Heavy Metals Map for location-specific guidance.
  - If air is the issue, adjust filtration and monitor conditions.
  - If children are exposed via soil, obtain and review testing/cleanup records.
  - For wells or local catch, save testing instructions and advisories, and consult healthcare or local agencies if exposure is suspected.

## Mercury Safety: A Team Report

This report summarizes key information regarding mercury safety, its health effects, and preventative measures.

### **Understanding Mercury and Its Forms**

Mercury is a naturally occurring element found in air, water, and soil, posing health risks primarily through human exposure. It exists in several forms, each with varying toxic effects [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).

*   **Elemental (Metallic) Mercury:**
    *   Mainly a risk from inhaling mercury vapor, often from industrial sources [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury/).
    *   Sources include thermometers, electrical switches, and dental amalgams [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [WHO AFRO](https://www.afro.who.int/sites/default/files/2026-10/Community%20Factsheet%20on%20Mercury.pdf).
*   **Inorganic Mercury Salts:**
    *   Exposure often through the gastrointestinal tract [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury/).
    *   Found in some cosmetics and pharmaceuticals [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [WHO AFRO](https://www.afro.who.int/sites/default/files/2026-10/Community%20Factsheet%20on%20Mercury.pdf).
*   **Organic Mercury (e.g., Methylmercury):**
    *   The most common exposure concern is from consuming contaminated fish and shellfish [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury/).
    *   Bioaccumulates in aquatic food webs, particularly in large predatory fish [HMAPP Foundation](https://hmapfoundation.org/heavy-metals-101/mercury-air-water-food/).
    *   Ethylmercury, used in some vaccines (thiomersal), does not pose health risks [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).

### **Health Effects of Mercury Exposure**

Mercury exposure is common, and all forms can have significant health impacts, particularly on developing fetuses and young children [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury/), [WHO AFRO](https://www.afro.who.int/sites/default/files/2026-10/Community%20Factsheet%20on%20Mercury.pdf/). Neurological and renal (kidney) toxicity are the most consistently observed outcomes [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).

*   **General Symptoms Across Forms:**
    *   Neurological: tremors, memory loss, cognitive/motor dysfunction, mood and behavioral changes, headaches, dizziness, poor coordination, speech/hearing/walking impairment [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury/), [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/), [WHO AFRO](https://www.afro.who.int/sites/default/files/2026-10/Community%20Factsheet%20on%20Mercury.pdf/), [GOB.PE](https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los-riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio).
    *   Renal (Kidney): kidney damage, decrements in kidney function, tubular and glomerular damage [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury/), [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/).
    *   Other: respiratory issues (cough, pneumonitis, edema), skin rashes, gastrointestinal damage, cardiovascular effects (blood pressure changes), and immune system activation [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury/), [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611012/), [WHO AFRO](https://www.afro.who.int/sites/default/files/2026-10/Community%20Factsheet%20on%20Mercury.pdf/).
*   **Specific Vulnerabilities:**
    *   **Fetuses and Young Children:** Most vulnerable to mercury's neurotoxic effects, leading to developmental issues, cognitive impairments, and behavioral disorders [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury/), [GOB.PE](https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los-riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio).
    *   **At-Risk Groups:** Health workers (dentists, lab staff), healthcare cleaners, waste handlers, users of skin-lightening products, and gold miners using mercury are at higher risk [WHO AFRO](https://www.afro.who.int/sites/default/files/2026-10/Community%20Factsheet%20on%20Mercury.pdf/).

### **Prevention and Safety Measures**

Reducing mercury exposure requires a multi-faceted approach, from industrial practices to individual actions.

*   **Reduce Industrial and Environmental Sources:**
    *   Eliminate mercury mining and reduce its use in gold extraction, promoting non-mercury alternatives [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
    *   Reduce emissions from coal-fired power plants and other industrial sources [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [HMAPP Foundation](https://hmapfoundation.org/heavy-metals-101/mercury-air-water-food/).
    *   Ensure safe disposal of mercury-containing waste and promote recycling [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [WHO AFRO](https://www.afro.who.int/sites/default/files/2026-10/Community%20Factsheet%20on%20Mercury.pdf/).
*   **Safe Handling and Product Alternatives:**
    *   Replace mercury-containing devices (thermometers, BP machines, electrical switches) with safer digital alternatives [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [WHO AFRO](https://www.afro.who.int/sites/default/files/2026-10/Community%20Factsheet%20on%20Mercury.pdf/), [GOB.PE](https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los-riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio).
    *   Avoid using cosmetics or other products that may contain inorganic mercury [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [GOB.PE](https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los-riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio).
    *   If mercury-containing items break, ventilate the area, do not use brooms or vacuums, and collect spheres with gloves and stiff paper into a hermetic container [GOB.PE](https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los-riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio).
*   **Dietary Guidance (Methylmercury):**
    *   Limit consumption of large, predatory fish (e.g., shark, swordfish, king mackerel) and local river fish known to accumulate mercury [GOB.PE](https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los-riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio).
    *   Prefer smaller fish, which typically have lower mercury levels [GOB.PE](https://www.gob.pe/108301-como-prevenir-los-riesgos-para-la-salud-por-exposicion-a-mercurio).
    *   Consult local fish advisories and seafood guides for lower-mercury options [HMAPP Foundation](https://hmapfoundation.org/heavy-metals-101/mercury-air-water-food/).
*   **General Precautions:**
    *   Wash hands after handling waste and avoid handling unidentified mercury-containing waste without personal protective equipment (PPE) [WHO AFRO](https://www.afro.who.int/sites/default/files/2026-10/Community%20Factsheet%20on%20Mercury.pdf/).
    *   Do not dispose of mercury-containing items in rivers, drains, or ordinary trash, and do not burn or bury them [WHO AFRO](https://www.afro.who.int/sites/default/files/2026-10/Community%20Factsheet%20on%20Mercury.pdf/).
    *   Test private water wells for contaminants if concerned [HMAPP Foundation](https://hmapfoundation.org/heavy-metals-101/mercury-air-water-food/).
    *   If exposure is suspected, seek prompt medical assessment and treatment [WHO AFRO](https://www.afro.who.int/sites/default/files/2026-10/Community%20Factsheet%20on%20Mercury.pdf/). Contact a physician or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury/).

Summary:
- Mercury exposes three chemical forms with overlapping health concerns, mainly neurological and renal effects across humans and animals.
- Elemental mercury (vapor):
  - Neurological effects in adults: tremor, vision and cognitive declines, slowed motor function, mood and behavioral changes.
  - Renal effects: decrements in kidney function; tubular and glomerular damage observed in animals and some human data.
  - Severe elemental mercury exposure can cause acute respiratory injury (pneumonitis, edema) and sometimes fatal outcomes.
- Inorganic mercury salts:
  - Neurological effects: developmental neurotoxicity (hyperactivity, impaired motor and memory, reduced sociability); adult neurobehavioral and motor impairments; overt signs in animals (ataxia, tremor, paralysis) and CNS changes.
  - Renal effects: dose- and duration-dependent nephrotoxicity (tubular and glomerular damage).
  - Cardiovascular effects: possible blood pressure and cardiac function changes.
  - Immunological and reproductive effects: immune activation in susceptible strains; impaired fertility and reduced sperm quality in animals.
  - Cancer: some evidence of male rat carcinogenicity (forestomach, thyroid); no clear human epidemiology.
- Cardiovascular findings (across mercury forms): some associations with increased blood pressure and altered cardiovascular function; evidence varies by exposure type (elemental, methylmercury, unspecified).
- Overall pattern: neurological and renal toxicity are the most consistently observed outcomes in both humans and animals; other organ systems show organ-specific or species-specific effects with more limited epidemiological support.

Summary:

- Mercury is a naturally occurring element found in air, water, and soil; human exposure occurs mainly via inhalation of mercury vapour (industrial) and consumption of contaminated fish and shellfish (methylmercury).
- All humans have some level of exposure. Mercury poses health risks, especially to fetal and early child development, and can affect the nervous, digestive, immune systems, lungs, kidneys, skin, and eyes.
- Mercury exists in several forms (elemental, inorganic, organic like methyl- and ethylmercury) with differing toxic effects. Methylmercury from fish is a key exposure concern; ethylmercury (in thiomersal) used in some vaccines does not pose health risks.
- Health impacts include neurological and behavioral disorders, tremors, memory loss, cognitive/motor dysfunction, kidney damage, and skin problems. Inorganic mercury salts are corrosive to skin/eyes and can cause kidney toxicity.
- Public health actions emphasized: eliminate mercury mining and reduce use in mining (especially artisanal small-scale gold mining); promote non-mercury gold extraction; recycle existing mercury; replace mercury-containing devices and products; reduce emissions from coal-fired power plants and other sources; ensure safe disposal and use of safer alternatives; vaccines with thiomersal are not a health risk.
- Common sources and products containing mercury include batteries, thermometers/other measuring devices, electrical switches, lamps, dental amalgams, cosmetics, and certain pharmaceuticals.

If you need a shorter one-liner: Mercury exposure is common and health-threatening, especially to fetal development; main risks come from methylmercury in fish and elemental mercury from industrial sources, with strong emphasis on reducing mercury use and exposure and clarifying vaccine thiomersal safety.

Mercury health effects depend on form (methylmercury, elemental/metallic, inorganic), dose, exposure duration, age (fetuses and young children are most vulnerable), and route of exposure. Key points:

- Methylmercury: most commonly from eating contaminated fish/shellfish. Most people have low body levels; high exposure can cause neurotoxic effects. Prenatal exposure can harm fetal brain/nervous system and later cognitive/behavioral functions. Possible symptoms: loss of peripheral vision, tingling, poor coordination, speech/hearing/walking impairment, and muscle weakness. If concerned, consult a physician.

- Metallic (elemental) mercury: risks mainly from inhaling mercury vapor. Symptoms with acute/long exposure include tremors, mood changes, insomnia, neuromuscular issues, headaches, sensory disturbances, cognitive decline; higher exposures can cause kidney damage, respiratory failure, or death.

- Inorganic mercury: high exposure can damage gastrointestinal tract, nervous system, kidneys; skin rashes, mood/memory changes, mental disturbances, muscle weakness. Absorption occurs via the GI tract.

- General guidance: exposure effects vary by form, dose, duration, age, and exposure route. Most people should consult a physician or poison control if exposure concerns arise (Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222). EPA drinking-water MCLs regulate inorganic mercury to prevent short- and long-term health risks.

Summary:

- Mercury exposure sources and routes:
  - Primary exposure: oral via contaminated food, especially methylmercury (MeHg) in fish/seafood; rice can contribute.
  - Minor exposures: contaminated water; elemental mercury from dental amalgams, older thermometers, and consumer products; inhalation and dermal routes also possible.
- Absorption:
  - Elemental Hg: well absorbed by inhalation; some absorption through skin and GI tract.
  - Inorganic Hg: absorbed via all routes; MeHg absorption through GI almost 100%; skin absorption possible.
- Distribution and metabolism:
  - Mercury distributes to the brain and kidneys; fetal transfer via cord blood, placenta, and breast milk.
  - Elemental Hg oxidized to Hg2+ in tissues; MeHg can be demethylated to Hg2+.
- Excretion:
  - Exhaled air (elemental Hg); urine and feces (Hg2+); hair (MeHg).
- Health effects:
  - Neurological: tremors, cognitive and sensory/motor impairments; effects depend on dose, duration, exposure route.
  - Prenatal: neurodevelopmental effects from MeHg exposure; possible birth defects at high dietary MeHg.
  - Renal: kidney injury from elemental Hg; tubular injury with exposure to inorganic/organic Hg.
  - Reproductive: impaired fertility in animals with oral inorganic/organic Hg.
  - Cardiovascular/immune: high blood pressure and immune function changes reported in some exposures.
- Regulatory/monitoring note:
  - ATSDR toxicological profile outlines exposure assessment, absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and health impact considerations for elemental, inorganic, and organic mercury compounds.

## Is Mercury Safe? A Team Report

Mercury is a highly toxic element that poses significant health risks to humans and the environment. Its safety depends heavily on the form of mercury, the level and duration of exposure, and individual vulnerabilities, particularly for fetuses and young children. Various national and international organizations like the EPA and WHO are actively working on reducing mercury exposure and its impact through regulations, public education, and promoting mercury-free alternatives.

### Health Risks of Mercury Exposure

Mercury is a neurotoxin that can severely impact the nervous, digestive, immune systems, kidneys, and other organs.

*   **Forms of Mercury and Their Effects:**
    *   **Elemental Mercury:** Primarily exposed through inhalation of vapors in industrial settings, dental amalgams, or broken thermometers. Symptoms include tremors, mood changes, insomnia, neuromuscular changes, headaches, and cognitive decline. High exposure can lead to kidney and lung damage, and can be fatal [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury/).
    *   **Inorganic Mercury:** Exposure can occur through various routes, causing gastrointestinal, nervous system, and kidney damage. Symptoms include skin dermatitis, mood/memory issues, mental disturbances, and muscle weakness [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury/), [ATSDR](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf).
    *   **Organic Mercury (Methylmercury):** The most common exposure pathway is consumption of contaminated fish and shellfish. Methylmercury is highly toxic and can lead to neurological, cognitive, and behavioral disorders, vision loss, tingling, poor coordination, and speech/hearing/walking impairments. It is especially dangerous for fetal brain and nervous system development, affecting cognition, memory, and motor skills [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury/), [ATSDR](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf).
    *   **Organic Mercury (Ethylmercury):** Found in thiomersal (a preservative), ethylmercury is generally not considered a health risk [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).

*   **Vulnerable Populations:** Fetuses and young children are most susceptible to the adverse effects of mercury exposure, especially methylmercury, which can lead to neurodevelopmental impairments [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury/), [ATSDR](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf).

*   **Exposure Pathways:**
    *   **Dietary:** Primarily through consumption of methylmercury in fish and shellfish, with rice also being a minor contributor [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [ATSDR](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf).
    *   **Inhalation:** Breathing in mercury vapor, particularly in industrial settings or from consumer products containing elemental mercury [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/), [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury/).
    *   **Other:** Minor exposures can occur through contaminated water, dental amalgams, and some consumer products [ATSDR](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf). Skin contact is also possible [ATSDR](https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/toxguides/toxguide-46.pdf).

### Regulations and Safety Guidelines

Organizations like the EPA and WHO implement various strategies to mitigate mercury risks and promote safer practices.

*   **EPA Initiatives:**
    *   **Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA):** A foundational act since 1976 that modernizes waste regulations to reduce permitting burdens, accelerate cleanups, and ensure safe management of hazardous waste, including mercury-containing products. RCRA protects millions and has facilitated the cleanup of vast contaminated land [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/epa-marks-50-years-resource-conservation-and-recovery-act-rcra-updates-modernize-waste).
    *   **Children's Health Publications:** The EPA provides resources such as "Protecting Children's Health Tips" and "Protect Children, Protect Our Future" to educate families about environmental health risks, including mercury, and offer practical steps to reduce exposure at home, school, and play [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/children/childrens-health-publications).
    *   **Drinking Water Standards:** The EPA sets Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) for mercury in drinking water to prevent health risks [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/mercury/health-effects-exposures-mercury/).

*   **WHO Initiatives:**
    *   **Global Mercury Reduction:** WHO advocates for the elimination of mercury mining, promotion of non-mercury gold extraction, switching to clean energy to reduce coal-related mercury emissions, and replacing mercury in medical devices [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health/).
    *   **Country-Specific Support:** WHO assists countries like Uganda in phasing out mercury-containing devices in health facilities by creating Information, Education and Communication (IEC) materials. These materials raise awareness, support policy changes, promote mercury-free alternatives, and help manage existing mercury devices [WHO](https://www.afro.who.int/countries/uganda/publication/mercury-reduction-information-education-and-communication-materials).

### Recommendations

*   **Reduce Exposure:** Limit consumption of high-mercury fish, avoid unnecessary use of mercury-containing products, and ensure proper disposal of mercury waste.
*   **Stay Informed:** Consult resources from the WHO, EPA, and ATSDR for up-to-date information on mercury risks and safety.
*   **Seek Medical Advice:** If you suspect mercury exposure or have concerns, contact a physician or poison control immediately.

Summary:

- Mercury exposure sources and routes:
  - Primary exposure: oral via contaminated food, especially methylmercury (MeHg) in fish/seafood; rice can contribute.
  - Minor exposures: contaminated water; elemental mercury from dental amalgams, older thermometers, and consumer products; inhalation and dermal routes also possible.
- Absorption:
  - Elemental Hg: well absorbed by inhalation; some absorption through skin and GI tract.
  - Inorganic Hg: absorbed via all routes; MeHg absorption through GI almost 100%; skin absorption possible.
- Distribution and metabolism:
  - Mercury distributes to the brain and kidneys; fetal transfer via cord blood, placenta, and breast milk.
  - Elemental Hg oxidized to Hg2+ in tissues; MeHg can be demethylated to Hg2+.
- Excretion:
  - Exhaled air (elemental Hg); urine and feces (Hg2+); hair (MeHg).
- Health effects:
  - Neurological: tremors, cognitive and sensory/motor impairments; effects depend on dose, duration, exposure route.
  - Prenatal: neurodevelopmental effects from MeHg exposure; possible birth defects at high dietary MeHg.
  - Renal: kidney injury from elemental Hg; tubular injury with exposure to inorganic/organic Hg.
  - Reproductive: impaired fertility in animals with oral inorganic/organic Hg.
  - Cardiovascular/immune: high blood pressure and immune function changes reported in some exposures.
- Regulatory/monitoring note:
  - ATSDR toxicological profile outlines exposure assessment, absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and health impact considerations for elemental, inorganic, and organic mercury compounds.

- Impact and collaboration: Prolific contributor with broad influence across representation theory, algebraic analysis, and mathematical physics; his methods continue to drive developments in multiple areas.

## Report: The 2025 Abel Prize in Mathematics

This report summarizes the contributions of the 2025 Abel Prize laureate in Mathematics, Masaki Kashiwara, and addresses the common misconception regarding a "Nobel Prize in Mathematics."

### 2025 Abel Prize Laureate: Masaki Kashiwara

Masaki Kashiwara, a Japanese mathematician, was awarded the 2025 Abel Prize "for his fundamental contributions to algebraic analysis and representation theory, in particular the development of the theory of D-modules and the discovery of crystal bases" [source](https://abelprize.no/article/2025/japanese-mathematician-masaki-kashiwara-awarded-abel-prize-2025). His work has had a broad and lasting impact across several areas of mathematics.

**Key Contributions Cited:**

*   **D-modules:** Kashiwara developed the theory of analytic D-modules, which provides an algebraic framework for linear partial differential equations (PDEs). This work introduced concepts like the characteristic variety and generalized the Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem [source](https://abelprisen.no/sites/default/files/2025-04/Citation_AbelPrize_2025_%20ENG_v2.pdf).
*   **Microlocal Analysis:** In collaboration with Pierre Schapira, he developed the microlocal analysis of sheaves, connecting differential equations on manifolds to geometry on the cotangent bundle. This established core concepts and clarified generic microlocal structures [source](https://abelprisen.no/sites/default/files/2025-04/Citation_AbelPrize_2025_%20ENG_v2.pdf).
*   **Riemann–Hilbert Correspondence:** Kashiwara formulated and proved a generalized correspondence between regular holonomic D-modules and perverse sheaves. This extended Deligne’s resolution to broader settings, with recent work further expanding this correspondence [source](https://abelprisen.no/sites/default/files/2025-04/Citation_AbelPrize_2025_%20ENG_v2.pdf).
*   **Kazhdan–Lusztig Theory and Representation Theory:** He co-developed the Kazhdan–Lusztig conjecture with Brylinski, linking representation characters to intersection cohomology via the Riemann–Hilbert framework. He also extended D-module methods to infinite-dimensional affine flag varieties with Tanisaki [source](https://abelprisen.no/sites/default/files/2025-04/Citation_AbelPrize_2025_%20ENG_v2.pdf).
*   **Quantum Groups and Crystal Bases:** Kashiwara introduced crystal graphs and constructed crystal and global bases, relating them to canonical bases. These provide pivotal combinatorial and structural tools in representation theory [source](https://abelprisen.no/sites/default/files/2025-04/Citation_AbelPrize_2025_%20ENG_v2.pdf).
*   **Impact and Collaboration:** Kashiwara is recognized for his prolific contributions, broad influence across algebraic analysis, representation theory, and mathematical physics, and his methods continue to drive developments in various areas [source](https://abelprisen.no/sites/default/files/2025-04/Citation_AbelPrize_2025_%20ENG_v2.pdf).

In summary, Kashiwara’s essential impact lies in creating and applying D-module and microlocal frameworks to solve deep problems in representation theory, notably the generalized Riemann–Hilbert correspondence and the development of crystal bases for quantum groups [source](https://abelprisen.no/sites/default/files/2025-04/Citation_AbelPrize_2025_%20ENG_v2.pdf).

### Clarification: The Abel Prize vs. The Nobel Prize

It is important to note that there is no "Nobel Prize in Mathematics." The award Kashiwara received is the Abel Prize, which is widely regarded as the equivalent of a Nobel Prize for mathematics.

**Reasons for No Nobel Prize in Mathematics:**

*   **Alfred Nobel's Will:** Alfred Nobel's will specifically outlined prizes for physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, and peace. Mathematics was not included in his scope of interest, which focused on fields with direct, tangible societal impact [source](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/the-prizes-rite/), [source](https://hsm.stackexchange.com/questions/24/why-isnt-there-a-nobel-prize-in-mathematics), [source](https://scilogs.spektrum.de/hlf/no-nobel-prize-for-mathematics-is-it-kovalevskayas-fault/).
*   **Existing Prizes:** At the time, other prestigious mathematical prizes already existed, such as one established by King Oscar II, potentially reducing the incentive for Nobel to create another [source](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/the-prizes-rite/).
*   **Focus on Practical Impact:** Nobel himself had interests in applied fields, and he may have deemed pure mathematics too theoretical or not yielding the practical benefits he sought for his prizes [source](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/the-prizes-rite/), [source](https://hsm.stackexchange.com/questions/24/why-isnt-there-a-nobel-prize-in-mathematics).
*   **Popular Myths Debunked:** The popular rumor that Nobel avoided a mathematics prize due to an affair with his wife is false; Alfred Nobel never married [source](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/the-prizes-rite/).

**Alternatives for Mathematics Recognition:**

*   **The Fields Medal:** This award serves as a top international mathematics award, though it is less lucrative than the Abel Prize [source](https://scilogs.spektrum.de/hlf/no-nobel-prize-for-mathematics-is-it-kovalevskayas-fault/).
*   **The Crafoord Prize:** Established in 1980, this prize fills a similar niche for mathematics, but it is less well-known and awarded by a different body [source](https://hsm.stackexchange.com/questions/24/why-isnt-there-a-nobel-prize-in-mathematics).
*   **The Abel Prize:** Established in 2003 by the Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters, the Abel Prize functions as a de facto Nobel for mathematics, providing significant recognition and financial reward [source](https://scilogs.spektrum.de/hlf/no-nobel-prize-for-mathematics-is-it-kovalevskayas-fault/).

## 2025 Nobel Prize in Mathematics: Committee Citation and Winner Contribution

### Absence of a Nobel Prize in Mathematics

There is no Nobel Prize in Mathematics. The Nobel Prizes are awarded in six categories: Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine, Literature, Peace, and Economic Sciences [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Nobel_Prizes), [source](https://telugu.newsbytesapp.com/news/science/why-is-there-no-nobel-prize-in-mathematics-the-truth-behind-the-love-story/story). Alfred Nobel did not include mathematics when establishing the prizes, and no definitive historical reason for this exclusion is documented (unverified), [source](https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/201501/rnoti-p15.pdf). A popular myth attributing the exclusion to a romantic vendetta by Alfred Nobel lacks credible evidence [source](https://telugu.newsbytesapp.com/news/science/why-is-there-no-nobel-prize-in-mathematics-the-truth-behind-the-love-story/story).

### Alternative Prestigious Awards in Mathematics

Despite the absence of a Nobel Prize, several prestigious awards recognize achievements in mathematics:

*   **Fields Medal:** Established in 1936, this award is given to mathematicians under 40 years old for particular contributions, rather than lifelong achievements [source](https://telugu.newsbytesapp.com/news/science/why-is-there-no-nobel-prize-in-mathematics-the-truth-behind-the-love-story/story), [source](https://www.ams.org/notices/201504/rnoti-p327.pdf). It was not originally intended for "the greatest mathematical genius" but rather to recognize promising young mathematicians whose careers would benefit from the recognition [source](https://www.science.org/content/article/fields-medal-was-never-meant-greatest-mathematical-genius). The age limit can influence research directions, and the "winner-takes-all" mentality can overshadow foundational contributions by others [source](https://www.ams.org/notices/201504/rnoti-p327.pdf).
*   **Abel Prize:** Established in 2003, the Abel Prize has no age limit and typically recognizes work across a longer career [source](https://telugu.newsbytesapp.com/news/science/why-is-there-no-nobel-prize-in-mathematics-the-truth-behind-the-love-story/story), [source](https://www.ams.org/notices/201504/rnoti-p327.pdf).
*   **Breakthrough Prize in Mathematics:** This annual award, funded by the Milner foundations and supported by figures like Mark Zuckerberg, honors outstanding achievements across diverse fields of mathematics, including topology, algebraic geometry, analysis, and number theory [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakthrough_Prize_in_Mathematics). Laureates receive a substantial cash prize ($3 million per award year) [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakthrough_Prize_in_Mathematics).

### 2025 Nobel Prize Laureates in Other Fields

For context, the 2025 Nobel Prizes recognized individuals in other categories for specific contributions:

*   **Physics:** John M. Martinis, with Michel Devoret and John Clarke, for macroscopic quantum tunneling and energy quantization in an electric circuit [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Nobel_Prizes).
*   **Chemistry:** Omar M. Yaghi, with Susumu Kitagawa and Richard Robson, for the development of metal–organic frameworks [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Nobel_Prizes).
*   **Physiology or Medicine:** Mary E. Brunkow, with Fred Ramsdell and Shimon Sakaguchi, for discoveries concerning peripheral immune tolerance [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Nobel_Prizes).
*   **Literature:** László Krasznahorkai, for his compelling and visionary body of work, affirming the power of art amid apocalyptic threat [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Nobel_Prizes).
*   **Peace:** María Corina Machado, for promoting democratic rights in Venezuela and advocating a peaceful transition from dictatorship to democracy [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Nobel_Prizes).
*   **Economic Sciences:** Joel Mokyr, with Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt, for insights into the prerequisites for sustained growth through technological progress and the theory of sustained growth via creative destruction (Aghion–Howitt model) [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Nobel_Prizes).

# Nobel Prize in Mathematics: 2025 Committee Citation

## Absence of a Nobel Prize in Mathematics

There is no Nobel Prize in Mathematics [source](https://www.nobelprize.org/frequently-asked-questions/). The Nobel Prizes were established by Alfred Nobel's will to honor those who have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind, funded by the interest from his fortune [source](https://www.nobelprize.org/frequently-asked-questions/). The original categories established in 1901 were Physics, Chemistry, Physiology/Medicine, Literature, and Peace [source](https://www.nobelprize.org/frequently-asked-questions/). The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel was added in 1968 as a memorial prize [source](https://www.nobelprize.org/frequently-asked-questions/).

The claim that no Nobel Prize exists for mathematics due to a supposed affair between a Swedish mathematician and Alfred Nobel’s wife is false, as Nobel never married [source](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/the-prizes-rite/). Possible explanations for the absence of a mathematics prize include Nobel’s own interests focusing on fields with more tangible impact on mankind, and the existence of a mathematics prize established by King Oscar II and Johan Mittag-Leffler in Sweden [source](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/the-prizes-rite/). The Nobel Prize has little historical connection to mathematics, partly because Nobel did not value or engage with mathematics [source](https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/201501/rnoti-p15.pdf).

## Equivalents to the Nobel Prize in Mathematics

While there is no Nobel Prize specifically for mathematics, several other prestigious awards are considered the highest honors in the field [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_awards_considered_the_highest_in_a_field). These include:

*   **Abel Prize** The Abel Prize is a Norwegian mathematics prize awarded by the Norwegian government, established in 2002 on the bicentennial of Niels Henrik Abel's birth [source](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagroda_Abela). It is funded by the Abel Foundation and currently has a value of approximately 980,000 USD [source](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagroda_Abela). The Abel Prize recognizes deep, significant mathematical contributions and can be awarded to single or multiple recipients [source](https://uwaterloo.ca/research/science-technology-engineering-and-math-awards). It is considered the mathematical equivalent of the Nobel Prize [source](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagroda_Abela). Laureates have been recognized for achievements in various mathematical fields, including topology, algebraic geometry, number theory, analysis, partial differential equations, group theory, probability, dynamics, geometry, discrete mathematics, and algebra [source](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagroda_Abela).

*   **Fields Medal** The Fields Medal is often considered the mathematical equivalent of the Nobel Prize, though it arose in a different political and social context and its status has been shaped by national interests and postwar international politics [source](https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/201501/rnoti-p15.pdf). The Fields Medal has historically favored white European and American men, reflecting broader inequities in access and recognition [source](https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/201501/rnoti-p15.pdf).

*   **Breakthrough Prize in Mathematics** Established in 2013, the Breakthrough Prize has categories for life sciences, fundamental physics, and mathematics [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_awards_considered_the_highest_in_a_field). It is noted for being very generous and has been called the “Oscars of Science” [source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_awards_considered_the_highest_in_a_field).

Given that there is no Nobel Prize in Mathematics, there would be no "2025 Nobel Prize in Mathematics committee" to cite a contribution for a winner. The information provided focuses on the absence of such a prize and the nature of its mathematical equivalents.
